::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 6) you can:

1. **write** the general message-passing framework (message → aggregate → update) and instantiate it for the basic GNN and the GCN;
2. **derive** the GCN layer twice — spatially (normalized neighborhood averaging, and why $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$ rather than a raw sum) and spectrally (graph Fourier transform → polynomial filters → first-order truncation);
3. **analyze** the propagation operators through their spectra: prove why the raw sum explodes, why the normalized operators stay bounded, and why repeated propagation smooths;
4. **prove** that a message-passing layer is permutation equivariant, that sum-pooling readout is permutation invariant, and exhibit graphs a message-passing GNN provably cannot distinguish;
5. **hand-simulate** one or two GCN layers on a small graph with given features — exactly the skill the midterm and final test;
6. **implement** GCN in about thirty lines of sparse PyTorch, state its time and memory complexity, and explain what every line does.
:::

## Why this lecture exists

Here is the concrete problem we carry through the whole lecture. The **Cora** graph
contains 2,708 machine-learning papers; each paper has a bag-of-words feature vector
(1,433 words) and citation links to the papers it cites; 140 papers — about 5% — carry a
topic label such as *neural networks* or *reinforcement learning*. Your job: label the
other 95%.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-cora-hero.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Commit to two numbers before reading on.** An MLP trained on the bag-of-words features
alone — every citation ignored: what test accuracy? And the model we build today, given
the same features *plus* the citations: how much better?

::: {.predict-answer}
The MLP lands near **60%** — and it plateaus there however much capacity you give it,
because the missing information simply is not in the features. Today's model reaches
about **82%**. Hold on to the pair 60/82: the gap *is* this lecture, and you will
reproduce both numbers yourself in the lab.
:::
:::

You already own two partial answers, and this lecture exists because both are wrong in
instructive ways:

- **Week 1's answer — use the features.** Train an MLP on the bag-of-words vectors and
  ignore the citations. This gets about **60%** accuracy on Cora. It never uses the one
  thing everyone believes about citation networks: papers cite papers on their own topic
  (<span class="term" data-def="Homophily: the tendency of connected nodes to share labels or attributes — 'birds of a feather'. The assumption that makes neighborhood averaging informative. Its opposite, heterophily, is where the GCN fails.">homophily</span>, from Week 1). Sixty percent is not an accident of a weak model — a stronger
  MLP, gradient boosting, anything feature-only plateaus in the same range, because the
  information simply is not all in the features.
- **Week 3's answer — use the structure.** Run label propagation: repeatedly average the
  label distribution of your neighbors. This uses the citations and nothing else — the
  bag-of-words vectors sit unused. And it can only *copy* information around; it cannot
  learn that the word "backprop" matters more than the word "therefore", cannot build
  intermediate representations, and has exactly zero trainable parameters with which to
  adapt to the task.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-three-answers.html >}}

The object of this week is the model that ends this dilemma by **learning how to
propagate features**: the graph neural network, and its most famous instance, the **graph
convolutional network** (GCN) of [Kipf & Welling, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907), which reaches about **82%** on
the same task with roughly 23,000 parameters. The twenty-two point jump over the MLP is
the measured value of structure; you will reproduce both numbers yourself in
[Lab 6](../labs/lab06.qmd).

A word on where this model came from, because the history *is* the structure of this
lecture. Neural networks on graphs were first proposed by Scarselli et al. around 2009 —
a recurrent scheme, iterated to a fixed point, largely ignored for a decade. The modern
line re-entered through **signal processing**: [Bruna et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6203) defined convolution on
graphs through the Laplacian's eigenbasis, [Defferrard et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.09375) made it cheap with
polynomial filters, and [Kipf & Welling, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907) truncated the polynomial to first order —
at which point the "spectral" model collapsed into a **spatial** rule so simple it reads
as "average your neighbors, then apply a shared linear map".

[Gilmer et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212)
then showed that this rule, GraphSAGE, GAT, and a zoo of chemistry models are all
instances of one template: **neural message passing**. That template is the single
framework behind essentially every architecture in the rest of this course — GraphSAGE,
GAT, and GIN next week are three different answers to *one design question inside*
today's framework, and RGCN in Week 10 is today's equations with typed edges.

**Roadmap.** (1) We turn label propagation into a learnable layer — the message-passing
framework. (2) We fix the arithmetic of aggregation — normalization — and prove, not just
observe, why the unnormalized sum explodes and the normalized operators do not.
(3) We re-derive the very same layer from the spectral direction — graph Fourier
transform, polynomial filters, first-order truncation — and extract the analysis that
view is uniquely good for: the GCN is a low-pass filter, with an oversmoothing theorem
already visible. (4) We prove the symmetry property that justifies the whole enterprise,
and meet the first graphs a message-passing network provably cannot tell apart. (5) We
write the code and count its costs.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
- **Adjacency matrix, degree matrix, Laplacian** ([Week 1](../syllabus.qmd)): $\mathbf{A}$,
  $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ for a graph with $n = |\mathcal{V}|$
  nodes and $m = |\mathcal{E}|$ edges, and the quadratic form
  $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2$
  measuring how much a signal varies across edges.
- **Eigendecomposition of symmetric matrices** (linear algebra): real eigenvalues,
  orthonormal eigenvectors, the Rayleigh quotient
  $R(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x} / \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}$
  bounded by the extreme eigenvalues.
- **Spectral clustering** ([Week 2](../syllabus.qmd)): the low Laplacian eigenvectors
  partition a graph into communities. Today they return as the "low frequencies" of a graph.
- **PageRank / power iteration** ([Week 2](../syllabus.qmd)): repeatedly applying a matrix
  amplifies its top eigendirection — today the same argument runs in reverse, as a
  failure mode.
- **Label propagation** ([Week 3](../syllabus.qmd)): iterate "become the average of your
  neighbors". Today's first section is precisely "label propagation, but learnable".
- **Homophily** (Week 1): connected nodes tend to share labels/attributes — the assumption
  that makes neighborhood averaging informative at all.
- From your ML course: MLPs, softmax + cross-entropy, backprop, dropout, weight sharing in CNNs.
:::

## 1. From propagation to message passing

Our cast graph from Week 1 stars in every diagram of this lecture — the colors let you
follow individual nodes through every construction, with $A$ as today's target:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-input-graph.html >}}

Label propagation repeats one primitive: *collect your neighbors' current values,
average them, adopt the average.* Three hard-coded choices hide in that sentence —
average (why not sum, or max, or a weighted combination?), adopt (why replace rather than
blend with what you already had?), and values (why propagate raw labels rather than some
learned representation of each node?). Message passing keeps the *shape* of the
computation and makes all three choices learnable.

::: {#def-mp .definition name="Neural message passing"}
A **message-passing layer** computes, for every node $u \in \mathcal{V}$ simultaneously,

$$
\mathbf{h}_u^{(k+1)} \;=\; \text{UPDATE}^{(k)}\!\Big(\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)},\;
\underbrace{\text{AGGREGATE}^{(k)}\big(\{\!\{\, \mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} : v \in \mathcal{N}(u) \,\}\!\}\big)}_{\textstyle =\; \mathbf{m}_{\mathcal{N}(u)}^{(k)}}\Big),
$$ {#eq-w06-mp}

where — $\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ is node $u$'s embedding after $k$
layers, $\mathbf{h}_u^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}_u$ (the input features);
$\mathcal{N}(u) = \{v : (u,v) \in \mathcal{E}\}$ is $u$'s neighborhood; $\{\!\{\cdot\}\!\}$ is a
<span class="term" data-def="Multiset: a collection where order is meaningless but repetition counts — {{a, a, b}} differs from {{a, b}} but not from {{b, a, a}}. Exactly the structure of 'my neighbors' vectors'.">*multiset*</span> (neighbors can contribute equal vectors, and there is no order), AGGREGATE is a
permutation-invariant function of that multiset, and UPDATE is any differentiable
function. After $K$ layers we take $\mathbf{z}_u = \mathbf{h}_u^{(K)}$.
:::

::: {.math-note}
Read it as a recipe: every node packs its current vector into a message, each node pools
the messages arriving from its neighborhood into one vector
$\mathbf{m}_{\mathcal{N}(u)}$, then combines that with its own state. One layer = one
round of this, everywhere at once.
:::

Here is @def-mp drawn out for node $A$ of our cast graph — read it right to left:
input features enter at layer 0, every gray box is one AGGREGATE + transform, and the
same picture exists for every node:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-comp-graph.html >}}

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-all-comp-graphs.html >}}

Three consequences are worth pausing on, because each becomes a theorem or a design axis
later in the course.

**First: information travels one hop per layer.** After $k$ layers,
$\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)}$ is a function of exactly the nodes within $k$ hops of $u$. The
object that makes this precise deserves a formal name:

::: {#def-w06-comp-tree .definition name="Computation tree"}
The **computation tree** of node $u$ for a $K$-layer message-passing model is the
depth-$K$ tree rooted at $u$: the root is $u$, its children are $\mathcal{N}(u)$, their
children are *their* neighbors (including $u$ itself — messages echo back), and the
leaves carry the input features. Read it as a completeness claim: everything a
$K$-layer GNN can ever know about $u$ is a function of this tree.
:::

::: {#def-w06-receptive .definition name="Receptive field"}
The **receptive field** of node $u$ in a $K$-layer message-passing GNN is the set of
input nodes that can influence $\mathbf{h}_u^{(K)}$ — exactly the $K$-hop neighborhood
of $u$, the node set of its computation tree. The word is borrowed from CNNs, where it
names the window of input pixels a unit sees; on a graph it grows one hop per layer.
:::

This pair of definitions will give us the equivariance proof in §4, the expressiveness
*ceiling* in §6 and Week 9 (two nodes with identical computation trees are
indistinguishable, full stop), and the scalability crisis in Week 11 (the tree's size
grows exponentially with $K$).

**Second: influence dilutes as it spreads.** How much does the input at node $v$ affect
the output at node $u$, $K$ layers later? For GCN-style models the answer has a clean
closed form — define the influence score

$$
I_K(u,v) \;=\; \mathbf{1}^\top \Big(\, \partial \mathbf{h}_u^{(K)} \big/ \partial \mathbf{h}_v^{(0)} \Big)\, \mathbf{1},
$$ {#eq-w06-influence}

where — $\partial \mathbf{h}_u^{(K)} / \partial \mathbf{h}_v^{(0)}$ is the Jacobian
matrix of $u$'s final embedding with respect to $v$'s input features, and
$\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones vector, so the expression sums the Jacobian's entries to
one number. This score
is proportional, in expectation, to the probability that a length-$K$ random walk from
$u$ ends at $v$ ([Hamilton, *GRL*](https://www.cs.mcgill.ca/~wlh/grl_book/), Theorem 3). Distant nodes are heard from, but at
random-walk volume — a fact that quantifies the "slow mixing" you can feel in Figure 1
and returns as oversmoothing in §3.

**Third: the same functions are applied at every node** — the graph analogue of a CNN
sliding one filter across every pixel. Parameters are shared, so the layer works on any
graph of any size, the parameter count is independent of $n$, and what is learned at one
node transfers to all others. Compare Week 3's shallow embeddings, which spent
$O(n \cdot d)$ parameters just to *name* the nodes, and could say nothing about a node
they had never seen.

::: {.predict}
**Before you touch the widget below:** every press of *Step* replaces each node's vector
with the average of its neighborhood. If you keep pressing forever, what happens to the
six vectors?

::: {.predict-answer}
They converge toward one shared vector — individuality drains out of the graph with
every round of averaging. Verify it below (eight or so steps make it obvious). This slow
death of information has a name, *oversmoothing*, and by §3 you will be able to prove it
and compute its rate.
:::
:::

Play with all three facts before we add parameters:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w6-message-passing.html >}}

The simplest concrete instance turns @def-mp into linear algebra:

::: {#def-basic .definition name="The basic GNN layer"}
$$
\mathbf{h}_u^{(k+1)} = \sigma\!\Big( \mathbf{W}_{\text{self}}^{(k)} \mathbf{h}_u^{(k)} + \mathbf{W}_{\text{neigh}}^{(k)} \!\!\sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)}\! \mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} + \mathbf{b}^{(k)} \Big),
$$ {#eq-w06-basic}

or, the same statement for all nodes at once,

$$
\mathbf{H}^{(k+1)} = \sigma\big(\mathbf{H}^{(k)}\mathbf{W}_{\text{self}}^{\top} + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{H}^{(k)}\mathbf{W}_{\text{neigh}}^{\top} + \mathbf{b}\big).
$$ {#eq-w06-basic-matrix}

where — $\mathbf{W}_{\text{self}}^{(k)}, \mathbf{W}_{\text{neigh}}^{(k)}$ are the two
learned weight matrices (transform yourself; transform your aggregated neighbors);
$\mathbf{b}^{(k)}$ is a learned bias vector (absorbed into the weights and dropped from
the prose hereafter); $\sigma$ is an elementwise nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU); and
$\mathbf{H}^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}$ stacks the embeddings as rows — the
convention throughout.
:::

::: {.math-note}
AGGREGATE = sum, UPDATE = a one-layer perceptron on [own state; aggregated neighbors].
The whole layer is two weight matrices (plus a bias). $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{H}$ is where the graph enters:
row $u$ of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{H}$ is exactly $\sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} \mathbf{h}_v$.
:::

A common simplification merges the two weight matrices by adding **self-loops**: replace
$\mathbf{A}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$, so every node is a
member of its own neighborhood and one matrix $\mathbf{W}$ suffices. We lose the ability
to treat "me" and "my neighbors" differently — a real loss we will revisit with GraphSAGE
next week, and one reason heterophilous graphs punish the GCN — and gain a pleasantly
short layer.

## 2. Getting the arithmetic right: normalization

@def-basic has a bug you can find without any machine learning, and — better — one you
can *prove*. A node with 500 neighbors receives a sum a hundred times larger than a node
with 5: feature scales become an accident of degree, gradients follow, and stacking
layers compounds the blow-up exponentially. Watch it happen, then let us see exactly how
fast "exponentially" is:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w6-normalization.html >}}

::: {#prp-spectra .proposition name="Spectra of the three propagation operators"}
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be connected with mean degree $\bar{d} = 2m/n$, and let
$\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$, $\tilde{\mathbf{D}} = \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{I}$.

1. **Sum:** $\lambda_{\max}(\tilde{\mathbf{A}}) \ge 1 + \bar{d}$. Repeated application
   multiplies a generic signal's norm by $\lambda_{\max}$ per step — exponential growth
   at least as fast as $(1 + \bar{d})^k$.
2. **Mean:** every eigenvalue of $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ lies in
   $[-1, 1]$, with $1$ attained by the constant vector — bounded forever.
3. **Symmetric (the GCN operator):** every eigenvalue of
   $\hat{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$
   lies in $(-1, 1]$, with $1$ attained by $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$ and $-1$
   **excluded** — the self-loops kill the bipartite oscillation that could otherwise reach $-1$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof</summary>
**(1)** The Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix lower-bounds its top eigenvalue at
any test vector. Take $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{1}$:
$R(\mathbf{1}) = \mathbf{1}^\top \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{1} / \mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{1} = (2m + n)/n = \bar{d} + 1$,
so $\lambda_{\max} \ge 1 + \bar{d}$. For a generic $\mathbf{h}$ (nonzero component along
the top eigenvector, which Perron–Frobenius — *a nonnegative irreducible matrix has a
simple top eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector* — guarantees is positive and hence not
orthogonal to generic nonnegative data), $\|\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^k \mathbf{h}\| = \Theta(\lambda_{\max}^k)$.

**(2)** $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ is row-stochastic (nonnegative, rows
sum to 1). For any eigenpair $(\lambda, \mathbf{v})$, pick $u$ maximizing $|v_u|$; then
$|\lambda| |v_u| = |\sum_v (\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{A}})_{uv} v_v| \le |v_u|$,
so $|\lambda| \le 1$; $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$.

**(3)** Upper end: $\mathbf{I} - \hat{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \tilde{\mathbf{L}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$
with $\tilde{\mathbf{L}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}} - \tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ the Laplacian of the
self-looped graph, which is PSD; hence $\lambda(\hat{\mathbf{A}}) \le 1$, attained by
$\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$ (check: $\hat{\mathbf{A}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{1} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{1} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$).
Lower end: for any $\mathbf{x}$, writing $\hat{x}_u = x_u / \sqrt{\tilde{d}_u}$,

$$
\mathbf{x}^\top (\mathbf{I} + \hat{\mathbf{A}}) \mathbf{x}
= \sum_{(u,v) \in \tilde{\mathcal{E}}} (\hat{x}_u + \hat{x}_v)^2 \;\ge\; 0,
$$

(sum over edges of the self-looped graph, self-loops contributing $(2\hat{x}_u)^2$ —
expand to verify: the cross terms rebuild $\mathbf{x}^\top \hat{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{x}$,
the squares rebuild $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}$). So $\lambda \ge -1$, with equality
forcing $\hat{x}_u = -\hat{x}_v$ on every edge *including* every self-loop
$(u,u)$ — which forces $\hat{x}_u = -\hat{x}_u = 0$ for all $u$. No eigenvector achieves
$-1$; the spectrum is contained in $(-1, 1]$. $\square$
</details>

::: {.math-note}
Part 3 is the mathematical content of the *renormalization trick* you will meet again in
@thm-gcn: adding self-loops **before** normalizing shrinks the spectrum from $[-1, 1]$
to $(-1, 1]$, so powers of the operator contract everywhere except along one benign
direction, instead of oscillating.
:::

With the spectra in hand, the design choice reads itself off. Two bounded options.
**Mean (random-walk) normalization** — every node averages its inbox:

$$
\mathbf{m}_{\mathcal{N}(u)} \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(u)|}\sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} \mathbf{h}_v,
$$ {#eq-w06-mean}

and **symmetric normalization**, which discounts each edge's message by the geometric
mean of the two endpoint degrees:

$$
\mathbf{m}_{\mathcal{N}(u)} \;=\; \sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} \frac{\mathbf{h}_v}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}(u)| \, |\mathcal{N}(v)|}}.
$$ {#eq-w06-sym}

where — $\mathbf{m}_{\mathcal{N}(u)}$ is the aggregated message of @eq-w06-mp,
$\mathbf{h}_v$ the neighbor's current embedding, and $|\mathcal{N}(u)|, |\mathcal{N}(v)|$
the receiver's and sender's degrees. @eq-w06-mean is bounded, simple, and exactly label
propagation's operator. In @eq-w06-sym a message is discounted both when the *receiver*
is popular and when the *sender* is: a citation from a 10,000-citation survey says less
about your topic than one from a focused 8-citation paper. On citation-like graphs this
hub-damping is consistently worth a couple of accuracy points, and — unlike the mean
operator — the symmetric operator is a similarity transform of a symmetric matrix, which
keeps its eigenvectors orthogonal and the spectral analysis of §3 clean.

Here is the mean-normalized layer with every term wired to the dataflow it denotes — the
anatomy to internalize before we compress it into matrix notation:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w6-eq-linked.html >}}

Symmetric normalization plus self-loops is the whole recipe:

::: {#def-gcn .definition name="The GCN layer (Kipf & Welling, 2017)"}
$$
\mathbf{H}^{(k+1)} \;=\; \sigma\!\big( \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \, \mathbf{H}^{(k)} \, \mathbf{W}^{(k)} \big),
\qquad \tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}, \quad \tilde{\mathbf{D}} = \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{I}.
$$ {#eq-w06-gcn}

where — $\mathbf{H}^{(k)}$ stacks the node embeddings as rows; $\mathbf{W}^{(k)}$ is the
layer's one learned matrix; $\tilde{\mathbf{A}}$ is the adjacency with self-loops added;
$\tilde{\mathbf{D}}$ its diagonal degree matrix; $\sigma$ an elementwise nonlinearity.
:::

::: {.math-note}
Everything left of $\mathbf{W}^{(k)}$ is fixed by the graph and computed once. Per
node — the exact equation Lab 6 implements and the exam simulates:

$$
\mathbf{h}_u^{(k+1)} \;=\; \sigma\Big(\mathbf{W}^{(k)\top} \!\!\sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cup \{u\}} \frac{\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)}}{\sqrt{\tilde{d}_u \tilde{d}_v}}\Big),
$$ {#eq-w06-gcn-node}

where — $\tilde{d}_u = |\mathcal{N}(u)| + 1$ is $u$'s self-looped degree (the diagonal
entry of $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}$), and the sum runs over the neighbors *plus $u$ itself*
(the self-loop).
:::

::: {#exm-hand .example name="Hand-simulation — the exam skill"}
Take the 4-node graph with edges $\{(A,B), (A,C), (B,C), (B,D)\}$, scalar features
$x_A = 2$, $x_B = -1$, $x_C = 3$, $x_D = 1$, and the mean-aggregation layer

$$
h_v^{(1)} \;=\; \mathrm{ReLU}\big( W \cdot \mathrm{mean}_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} h_u^{(0)} + B \cdot h_v^{(0)} \big),
$$ {#eq-w06-handrule}

where — $W$ weighs the neighborhood mean and $B$ weighs the node's own value (both
scalars here, matrices in general); take $W = B = 1$ (no self-loop in the mean). Then:

| node | neighbors | mean of neighbors | + own | ReLU |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $A$ | $B, C$ | $(-1+3)/2 = 1$ | $1 + 2 = 3$ | $\mathbf{3}$ |
| $B$ | $A, C, D$ | $(2+3+1)/3 = 2$ | $2 - 1 = 1$ | $\mathbf{1}$ |
| $C$ | $A, B$ | $(2-1)/2 = 0.5$ | $0.5 + 3 = 3.5$ | $\mathbf{3.5}$ |
| $D$ | $B$ | $-1$ | $-1 + 1 = 0$ | $\mathbf{0}$ |

Note $D$: the ReLU clipped it to zero — one round of aggregation can *erase* a node's
signal, which is why nonlinearities make these models more than fancy averaging. On the
midterm you will do exactly this, on a fresh graph, possibly for two layers — practice
until it is mechanical.
:::

::: {#exm-matrix .example name="The same computation, matrix form"}
The per-node table above is one matrix identity. With
$\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A}$ (row-stochastic, Week 2's random-walk operator)
and $\mathbf{x} = (2, -1, 3, 1)^\top$:

$$
\mathbf{h}^{(1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}\big( \mathbf{P}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x} \big)
= \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0.5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right)
= \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 3.5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The exam will accept either route; the matrix route is faster and self-checking (compute
$\mathbf{P}$ once, reuse it for layer two). For a *second* layer, feed
$\mathbf{h}^{(1)}$ back in: $\mathbf{h}^{(2)} = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{h}^{(1)} + \mathbf{h}^{(1)})$
— self-check question Q2 asks you for one of its entries.
:::

### Cost accounting, once and honestly

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-matrix-pipeline.html >}}

Every GCN layer is two matrix products, and their costs are not symmetric — write $d$
for the layer's input width and $d'$ for its output width:

- $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}$ — mixing channels: $O(n \, d \, d')$ time, dense but small.
- $\hat{\mathbf{A}} \cdot (\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W})$ — propagating: $O(m \, d')$ time if
  $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ is stored sparse (one multiply–add per edge per channel), but
  $O(n^2 d')$ if you foolishly store it dense.

For Cora ($n = 2{,}708$, $m \approx 10{,}556$ directed edges, $d = 1{,}433$,
hidden $16$): the *feature mixing* dominates — about $62$M multiply–adds — while sparse
propagation is a mere $0.2$M. Memory is $O(nd + m)$. Two lessons: sparsity is not an
optimization, it is the difference between linear and quadratic in $n$ (Lab 6 makes you
measure it); and on small graphs the graph part of a GNN is nearly free — the MLP inside
is what you are paying for.

## 3. The spectral view: why "convolutional"?

Nothing so far explains the name graph *convolutional* network. The answer comes from
running the CNN analogy properly, and it earns its place twice over: it is where the
architecture historically came from, and it is the sharpest *analysis* tool we have —
by the end of this section the GCN's failure modes (oversmoothing, heterophily) will be
visible in one picture. This is also the mathematics behind positional encodings
(Week 13) and half of the graph signal processing literature.

On images, convolution has an equivalent definition in the frequency domain: convolving
with a filter equals multiplying the image's Fourier coefficients by the filter's
frequency response, and the Fourier basis exists because the pixel grid has translation
symmetry. Graphs have no translations — but they have the Laplacian, the Laplacian is
symmetric, and symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenbases. That eigenbasis will play
the role of the Fourier basis, and the justification is more than an analogy: on a ring
graph (the discretized circle) the Laplacian eigenvectors *are* the discrete sines and
cosines,

$$
u_k(j) \;\propto\; \cos\!\big(2\pi k j / n\big),
\qquad \lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos\!\big(2\pi k / n\big),
$$ {#eq-w06-ring}

where — $u_k(j)$ is the $k$-th eigenvector's value at node $j$, $n$ the ring's node
count, $\lambda_k$ the matching eigenvalue — classical Fourier
analysis is literally the special case where the graph is a cycle. Try
the `ring` option in Figure 4 and watch the sinusoids appear.

::: {#def-gft .definition name="Graph Fourier transform"}
Let $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top$ be the eigendecomposition
of the Laplacian of an undirected graph, eigenvalues
$0 = \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_n$, orthonormal eigenvectors
$\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_n$. For a **graph signal** $\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^n$
(one number per node), its **graph Fourier transform** is
$\hat{\mathbf{f}} = \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{f}$, and $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{U}\hat{\mathbf{f}}$
reconstructs it: every signal is a weighted sum of eigenvectors, $\hat{f}_k$ the weight
on the $k$-th.
:::

::: {.math-note}
Nothing mystical happened: we chose an orthonormal basis adapted to the graph and wrote
signals in its coordinates. The content is in *which* basis — the next result says the
Laplacian's eigenbasis is ordered by smoothness, which is what "frequency" means here.
:::

::: {#prp-freq .proposition name="Eigenvalues are frequencies"}
For a signal $\mathbf{x}$, the Laplacian quadratic form measures total
variation across edges:

$$
\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} \;=\; \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{E}} (x_u - x_v)^2,
$$ {#eq-w06-tv}

where — $x_u$ is the signal's value at node $u$ and the sum runs over the edge set
$\mathcal{E}$: smooth signals score low. By Courant–Fischer (the min–max characterization of a symmetric matrix's
eigenvalues: the $k$-th smallest is the minimum of the quadratic form over unit vectors
orthogonal to the first $k-1$ eigenvectors),

$$
\lambda_k \;=\; \min_{\substack{\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_{k-1} \\ \|\mathbf{x}\| = 1}} \; \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x},
$$

so $\mathbf{u}_k$ is the *smoothest possible signal orthogonal to all smoother ones*:
$\mathbf{u}_1 \propto \mathbf{1}$ is constant ($\lambda_1 = 0$), $\mathbf{u}_2$ is
Week 2's spectral-clustering direction (the smoothest way to be non-constant — it varies
*between* communities and barely *within* them), and high-$k$ eigenvectors oscillate
across individual edges. Low $\lambda$ = smooth = low frequency.
:::

The whole proposition in one picture — smooth eigenvectors on the left of the spectrum,
oscillation on the right, and (previewing where this section ends) the GCN's response
laid over the top:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-spectrum.html >}}

Experiment with all of this — the eigenvector gallery in Figure 4 is this proposition
made visible:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w6-spectral.html >}}

A **spectral filter** now does on graphs what a convolution does on images: rescale each
frequency component by a response $g(\lambda)$,

$$
\mathbf{f} \;\mapsto\; \mathbf{U} \, g(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \, \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{f},
\qquad g(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) = \mathrm{diag}\big(g(\lambda_1), \dots, g(\lambda_n)\big).
$$ {#eq-w06-filter}

where — $\mathbf{f}$ is a graph signal, $\mathbf{U}$ the Laplacian's eigenvector matrix
(@def-gft), and $g : \lambda \mapsto g(\lambda)$ the **frequency response**, applied to
each eigenvalue separately.

Learning an arbitrary response value per eigenvalue (Bruna et al., 2014) is the most
expressive version of this idea, and it fails on all three engineering axes at once: it
needs the full eigendecomposition ($O(n^3)$ once), applying the filter is dense
($O(n^2)$ per signal), and — worst — the learned coefficients are glued to one specific
graph's eigenbasis, so the filter cannot transfer to any other graph, and is not even
guaranteed to be spatially localized on its own graph. All three problems disappear if we
restrict $g$ to a **polynomial**:

::: {#prp-poly .proposition name="Polynomial filters are local and cheap"}
If $g_w(\lambda) = \sum_{i=0}^{K} w_i \lambda^i$ with learned coefficients
$w_0, \dots, w_K$, then

$$
\mathbf{U} \, g_w(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \, \mathbf{U}^\top \;=\; g_w(\mathbf{L}) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^K w_i \mathbf{L}^i:
$$ {#eq-w06-poly}

no eigendecomposition is needed, each application costs $K$ sparse multiplies
($O(K \cdot m)$), the parameter count is $K + 1$ regardless of the graph's size, and the
filtered value at node $u$ depends only on nodes within $K$ hops of $u$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof</summary>
For any polynomial, $g_w(\mathbf{L}) = g_w(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top) = \mathbf{U} g_w(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{U}^\top$
because $(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top)^i = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^i\mathbf{U}^\top$
by $\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{I}$, and matrix polynomials distribute over this.
Locality: $(\mathbf{L}^i)_{uv} \ne 0$ requires a walk of length $\le i$ from $u$ to $v$
(induction on $i$: $\mathbf{L}$ has the sparsity pattern of $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$),
so the $K$-th order filter reads at most the $K$-hop neighborhood. $\square$
</details>

ChebNet (Defferrard et al., 2016) is this idea made numerically sound: instead of raw
monomials $\lambda^i$ (whose values explode across $[0, \lambda_{\max}]$ and produce
badly conditioned optimization), expand in **Chebyshev polynomials**

$$
T_0(x) = 1, \qquad T_1(x) = x, \qquad T_{i}(x) = 2x\,T_{i-1}(x) - T_{i-2}(x),
$$ {#eq-w06-cheb}

where — $T_i$ is the degree-$i$ Chebyshev polynomial and $x$ ranges over the rescaled
spectrum $\tilde{\lambda} \in [-1, 1]$ — an orthogonal basis, bounded by $1$ in absolute
value, computable by the same sparse recurrence. The GCN is one more, far more
aggressive, simplification away:

::: {#thm-gcn .theorem name="GCN is a first-order spectral filter"}
Truncate the Chebyshev filter at $K = 1$ over the normalized Laplacian
$\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}}$, approximate $\lambda_{\max} \approx 2$, and tie the two
remaining coefficients as $w = w_0 = -w_1$. The filter collapses to

$$
g_w(\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}})\,\mathbf{x} \;\approx\; w \big( \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2} \big)\, \mathbf{x},
$$

and replacing $\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$ (spectrum in
$[0,2]$, so repeated application is unstable) by
$\hat{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$
(spectrum in $(-1,1]$ by @prp-spectra) — the **renormalization trick** — gives exactly
the GCN layer of @def-gcn, applied featurewise with a learned mixing matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
:::

<details><summary>Derivation (complete)</summary>
Start from the order-1 Chebyshev expansion on the rescaled Laplacian
$\tilde{\mathbf{L}} = \tfrac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}} - \mathbf{I}$:

$$
g(\tilde{\mathbf{L}}) \;\approx\; w_0 T_0(\tilde{\mathbf{L}}) + w_1 T_1(\tilde{\mathbf{L}}) \;=\; w_0 \mathbf{I} + w_1 \tilde{\mathbf{L}}.
$$

With $\lambda_{\max} \approx 2$ (exactly $2$ iff the graph is bipartite; near $2$ for
many real graphs; an approximation the learned weights absorb),
$\tilde{\mathbf{L}} \approx \mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}} - \mathbf{I} = -\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$,
using $\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$. So

$$
g(\mathbf{L}_{\text{sym}}) \;\approx\; w_0 \mathbf{I} - w_1 \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}.
$$

Setting $w = w_0 = -w_1$ (one parameter per filter instead of two — fewer parameters,
less overfitting, and empirically no loss): $g \approx w(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2})$.
That operator's spectrum lies in $[0, 2]$; stacking $k$ layers powers it $k$ times, so
components at eigenvalue $2$ grow as $2^k$ — numerically unstable. The renormalization
$\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbf{A}}$
adds the self-loops *before* normalizing; @prp-spectra places $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$'s
spectrum in $(-1, 1]$, so repeated application contracts instead of exploding. Apply the
scalar filter independently to each of $d$ input feature channels and mix channels with a
learned $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}$, add $\sigma$, and @def-gcn appears. $\square$
</details>

### What the spectral view buys: the GCN is a low-pass filter

After @thm-gcn, the GCN's fixed propagation is one specific filter response — the
"low-pass" claim itself, in one line:

$$
g(\tilde{\lambda}) \;=\; 1 - \tilde{\lambda},
$$ {#eq-w06-response}

where — $\tilde{\lambda} \in [0, 2)$ is an eigenvalue of the *self-looped* normalized
Laplacian $\tilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\text{sym}} = \mathbf{I} - \hat{\mathbf{A}}$, so
$1 - \tilde{\lambda}$ is the matching eigenvalue of $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ — the response is
large at low frequencies, small or sign-flipping at high ones. Repeated application
sharpens that preference into a theorem:

::: {#prp-lowpass .proposition name="Repeated propagation is low-pass — oversmoothing, quantitatively"}
Let $\hat{\mathbf{A}} = \sum_i \mu_i \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top$ be the
eigendecomposition of the GCN operator on a connected graph, $1 = \mu_1 > \mu_2 \ge
\dots \ge \mu_n > -1$ (top eigenvalue simple by Perron–Frobenius: $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ is
nonnegative, irreducible, and the self-loops make it aperiodic). Then for any signal
$\mathbf{x}$,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{A}}^k \mathbf{x} \;=\; \sum_i \mu_i^k \langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{x} \rangle\, \mathbf{v}_i
\;\xrightarrow{\;k \to \infty\;}\; \langle \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{x} \rangle\, \mathbf{v}_1,
\qquad \mathbf{v}_1 \propto \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1},
$$ {#eq-w06-lowpass}

where — $\mu_i, \mathbf{v}_i$ are the eigenpairs named above,
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product, and the error shrinks as
$|\mu_2|^k$. Propagation without learning converges to a
*degree-scaled constant*: every node's representation becomes the same number times
$\sqrt{\tilde{d}_u}$ — all feature information gone, only degrees left.
:::

<details><summary>Proof</summary>
Expand $\mathbf{x} = \sum_i \langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{x}\rangle \mathbf{v}_i$ in the
orthonormal eigenbasis and apply $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^k$ termwise:
$\hat{\mathbf{A}}^k \mathbf{v}_i = \mu_i^k \mathbf{v}_i$. By @prp-spectra all
$|\mu_i| \le 1$ with $\mu_1 = 1$ attained by $\mathbf{v}_1 \propto \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{1/2}\mathbf{1}$
and $-1$ excluded; simplicity of $\mu_1$ (Perron–Frobenius for irreducible aperiodic
nonnegative matrices, up to the diagonal similarity $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{\pm 1/2}$) gives
$|\mu_i| < 1$ for $i \ge 2$, so every term except the first decays geometrically, at rate
$|\mu_2|^k$. $\square$
</details>

::: {.math-note}
This is Week 9's oversmoothing theorem in embryo. Trainable weights and ReLUs make the
full story subtler — but not better: in practice a deep GCN's representations still
collapse, and you watched exactly this happen in Figure 1. The spectral gap
$1 - |\mu_2|$ controls the speed: small-world graphs mix fast, so even 4–6 layers can be
too many.
:::

Two honest remarks the field learned the hard way — both of them things you should be
able to say out loud in an interview.

*First*, after this section the GCN is best understood as a **fixed low-pass filter plus
a learned channel mix**: it smooths features over neighborhoods, which is precisely
right under homophily — and precisely wrong without it. Don't take our word for it. SGC
([Wu et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07153); in the optional reading) makes the
point brutally: delete every nonlinearity, precompute $\hat{\mathbf{A}}^K \mathbf{X}$
once, fit logistic regression, and match the GCN on Cora — @alg-w06-sgc is the whole
method.

::: {#alg-w06-sgc .algorithm name="SGC: precompute, then logistic regression"}
Computes GCN-quality node predictions with no message passing at training time.

**Input:** features $\mathbf{X}$; sparse $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$; depth $K$; labeled set $\mathcal{V}_{\text{train}}$ with labels $y$. **Output:** class predictions for all $n$ nodes.

1. $\bar{\mathbf{X}} \leftarrow \mathbf{X}$
2. **for** $k = 1, \dots, K$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\bar{\mathbf{X}} \leftarrow \hat{\mathbf{A}}\, \bar{\mathbf{X}}$
4. **end for**
5. fit logistic regression $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ on $\{(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_u, y_u) : u \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{train}}\}$
6. **return** $\mathrm{softmax}(\bar{\mathbf{X}} \boldsymbol{\Theta})$
:::

Steps 2–4 are the entire "GNN": $K$ sparse multiplies costing $O(K m d)$ in total, run
*once, offline*, before any training. Step 5 is a plain linear classifier — in Lab 6, a
single linear layer trained with cross-entropy: exactly multinomial logistic regression.
The low-pass filter, not the "neural network", is doing most of the work on these
benchmarks — you will run this experiment yourself in Lab 6 and decide how you feel
about it.

*Second*, general spectral architectures lost to spatial message passing not because the
mathematics fails but because the engineering does: eigenbases do not transfer across
graphs, and $O(n^2)$ does not scale. The spectral *view* survives everywhere; spectral
*architectures* mostly did not. When someone asks why your GNN has "convolutional" in
its name, this section is the answer.

The low-pass bet, drawn out — the single picture to recall whenever someone hands you a
new graph dataset:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-homophily.html >}}

## 4. The symmetry that makes it all legal

We keep saying "the same function at every node". The formal property doing the work
deserves its own definitions — they reappear in every architecture we will meet, and in
Week 13 they become the organizing principle of the whole field. Start from the picture:
one graph, two storage orders, two adjacency matrices —

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-permutation.html >}}

::: {#def-perm .definition name="Permutation invariance and equivariance"}
Let $\mathbf{P}_\pi$ be any $n \times n$ permutation matrix. A function $f$ of a graph is
**permutation invariant** if
$f(\mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top,\, \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{X}) = f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{X})$
(the output ignores node ordering — right for graph-level predictions), and
**permutation equivariant** if
$f(\mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top,\, \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{P}_\pi\, f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{X})$
(the outputs travel with the nodes — right for node-level predictions).
:::

::: {#thm-equiv .theorem name="GCN layers are permutation equivariant"}
The GCN layer $f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{H}) = \sigma\big(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\,\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}\big)$
is permutation equivariant. Consequently a stack of GCN layers is equivariant, and
composing it with a sum readout $\mathbf{z}_{\mathcal{G}} = \sum_u \mathbf{h}^{(K)}_u$ —
the sum of all final-layer node embeddings —
yields a permutation-invariant graph-level model.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (short and worth reading)</summary>
Write $\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{A})$ for the normalized operator built from $\mathbf{A}$.
Permuting relabels rows and columns together, so degrees follow their nodes:
$\tilde{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top) = \mathbf{P}_\pi \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top$
and
$\tilde{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top) = \mathbf{P}_\pi \tilde{\mathbf{D}} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top$,
hence (using $\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top \mathbf{P}_\pi = \mathbf{I}$ and
$(\mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{M} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top)^{-1/2} = \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{M}^{-1/2} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top$
for diagonal positive $\mathbf{M}$)
$\hat{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top) = \mathbf{P}_\pi \hat{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top$.
Then

$$
f(\mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top, \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{H})
= \sigma(\mathbf{P}_\pi \hat{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{P}_\pi^\top \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W})
= \sigma(\mathbf{P}_\pi \hat{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W})
= \mathbf{P}_\pi \sigma(\hat{\mathbf{A}} \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W})
= \mathbf{P}_\pi f(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{H}),
$$

the elementwise $\sigma$ commuting with row permutation. Composition of equivariant maps
is equivariant (chain the identity). For the readout,
$\sum_u (\mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{H})_u = \sum_u \mathbf{H}_u$: a sum does not care about
order, so the composed graph-level model is invariant. $\square$
</details>

::: {.math-note}
Note what the proof does **not** allow: any operation that addresses node *indices*
rather than node *values* — "zero out row 1", "concatenate node 3's features", a
per-node learned embedding table. Appending unique IDs to features buys expressive power
(Week 9's higher-order models do a disciplined version of exactly this) at the price of
this theorem, and the price is real: the model can then memorize storage order.
:::

Why insist? Because node ordering in an adjacency matrix is *storage*, not *information*:
the same 5-node graph has up to $5! = 120$ different adjacency matrices. A model whose
output changes under reordering — say, an MLP fed the flattened matrix — is fitting
storage artifacts; and since the orderings are combinatorially many, no amount of data
augmentation truly fixes it.

Equivariance is also a *statistical* statement: it is the
inductive bias that shrinks the hypothesis space to functions of the graph itself, the
exact analogue of a CNN's translation weight-sharing — and, as with CNNs, it is why the
parameter count does not grow with the input size.

::: {.predict}
**Two predictions before the widget:** I shuffle the storage order of the same graph.
(1) The GNN's output for each *named node* — change or hold? (2) The MLP's score computed
from the flattened adjacency matrix — change or hold?

::: {.predict-answer}
The GNN's outputs **hold** — each value travels with its node identity, exactly what
@thm-equiv promises. The MLP's score **changes**: it was reading storage order, not the
graph. If you predicted both correctly, you already understand equivariance; the widget
below lets you catch the MLP in the act as many times as you like.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/d3/w6-permutation.html >}}

This is the deepest idea of the week, and it generalizes: CNNs are the same story with
*translation* symmetry on a grid graph, Transformers are attentional message passing on a
complete graph with positions as features, and DeepSets is the edgeless special case.
Architectures = symmetries. We pull that thread properly in Week 13.

## 5. The GCN in code, trained honestly

The entire model for Cora is two GCN layers ([Kipf & Welling, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907)).
In Lab 6 you will implement this model yourself, starting from an empty
file; @alg-w06-gcn-forward is line-for-line the specification of the
`GCN.forward` you will write:

::: {#alg-w06-gcn-forward .algorithm name="Two-layer GCN forward pass"}
Computes class logits for every node from the features and the fixed propagation
operator.

**Input:** features $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$; sparse $\hat{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$; weights $\mathbf{W}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}$, $\mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times C}$ ($C$ classes); dropout rate $p$. **Output:** logits $\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times C}$.

1. $\mathbf{H} \leftarrow \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_1$
2. $\mathbf{H} \leftarrow \hat{\mathbf{A}}\,\mathbf{H}$
3. $\mathbf{H} \leftarrow \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{H})$
4. $\mathbf{H} \leftarrow \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathbf{H}, p)$ — training only
5. $\mathbf{Z} \leftarrow \hat{\mathbf{A}}\,(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}_2)$
6. **return** $\mathbf{Z}$ — softmax lives inside the loss
:::

Steps 1–2 are one GCN layer of @eq-w06-gcn in the cheap order: mix channels first
($O(n\,d\,d')$, dense), then propagate one hop ($O(m\,d')$, sparse). Step 4 is the main
regularizer; step 5 repeats the pair for the output layer. In code:

```python
class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_feats, hidden, num_classes, p_drop=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.W1 = torch.nn.Linear(num_feats, hidden, bias=False)
        self.W2 = torch.nn.Linear(hidden, num_classes, bias=False)
        self.p = p_drop

    def forward(self, X, A_hat):            # A_hat: sparse D̃^-1/2 Ã D̃^-1/2, built once
        H = torch.relu(A_hat @ self.W1(X))     # layer 1: mix channels, propagate, ReLU
        H = torch.nn.functional.dropout(H, self.p, self.training)
        return A_hat @ self.W2(H)              # layer 2: logits; softmax lives in the loss
```

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-gcn-pipeline.html >}}

Training is standard cross-entropy **on the labeled nodes only**. With
$\mathcal{V}_{\text{train}}$ the 140 labeled nodes and $\mathbf{Z} = f(\mathbf{X}, \hat{\mathbf{A}})$
the logits,

$$
\mathcal{L} \;=\; - \sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{train}}} \log \frac{\exp(Z_{u, y_u})}{\sum_c \exp(Z_{u, c})},
$$ {#eq-w06-loss}

where — $y_u$ is node $u$'s ground-truth label, $c$ ranges over the 7 topic classes, and
$Z_{u,c}$ is the logit for class $c$ at node $u$.

::: {.math-note}
The sum runs over 140 nodes, but the forward pass runs over all 2,708: every unlabeled
node participates in propagation, shaping the representations of its labeled neighbors —
this is what makes the setting genuinely <span class="term" data-def="Semi-supervised: the model trains its loss on a few labeled examples while the unlabeled data still participates in the computation (here: through propagation). Different from small-sample supervised learning, where unlabeled data is simply absent.">*semi-supervised*</span> rather than just
small-sample. Q1 in the self-check asks you to point at the line of code where the
unlabeled nodes enter.
:::

The hyperparameters that reproduce the paper, and that you should treat as the default
starting point for any citation-scale graph:

| knob | value | why |
|---|---|---|
| hidden width | 16 | Cora is small; wider mostly overfits |
| depth | 2 | receptive field of 2 hops; deeper hurts (@prp-lowpass) |
| dropout | 0.5 on hidden layer | the main regularizer |
| optimizer | Adam, lr $10^{-2}$ | |
| weight decay | $5 \times 10^{-4}$ (first layer) | features are 1,433-dim and sparse |
| epochs | 100–200, early stop on validation | convergence is fast |

Parameter count: $1433 \times 16 + 16 \times 7 = 23{,}040$ — smaller than one modern
embedding table row count, and *independent of $n$* by weight sharing (§4).

::: {.margin-note}
**Where this exact pattern earns money.** Neighborhood aggregation with shared weights is
the core of [PinSage](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973) (Pinterest's 3-billion-node recommender), of [Google Maps' ETA model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11482)
(road segments aggregating traffic from neighbors), and of the fraud-detection GNNs at
every major payments company. When you implement Lab 6 you are writing the same ten
lines those systems scale up. The differences — sampling, serving, feature stores — are
Weeks 11 and 14.
:::

## 6. What the GCN cannot see

Before you leave believing message passing is the end of history, here is a five-line
proof that it is not.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-triangles-hexagon.html >}}

::: {#exm-limits .example name="Two graphs no message-passing GNN can distinguish"}
Let $\mathcal{G}_1$ be two disjoint triangles and $\mathcal{G}_2$ a single 6-cycle, all
twelve nodes carrying the same initial feature $\mathbf{x}$. Both graphs are 2-regular.
Claim: *every* message-passing GNN (any AGGREGATE, any UPDATE, any depth) assigns them
identical graph-level embeddings under sum readout.

*Proof.* By induction on the layer. At $k = 0$ all nodes in both graphs share the same
vector. If at layer $k$ every node in both graphs has the same vector
$\mathbf{h}^{(k)}$, then every node — in either graph — sees the identical multiset
$\{\!\{\mathbf{h}^{(k)}, \mathbf{h}^{(k)}\}\!\}$ (two neighbors, both carrying
$\mathbf{h}^{(k)}$), so UPDATE produces the same $\mathbf{h}^{(k+1)}$ everywhere. By
induction all nodes agree at every layer; both readouts equal
$6\,\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{h}^{(K)})$. $\square$
:::

::: {.math-note}
The stakes are not academic: "two 3-rings vs one 6-ring" is a real distinction between
molecules. The failure is structural — both graphs generate identical computation trees
(§1) — and no width, depth, or training regime fixes it. What *does* fix it (better
aggregators reaching the WL ceiling, structural features, higher-order message passing)
is exactly Week 9's subject; Week 13's positional encodings are another escape route.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · “Each node learns its own weights”" icon="false"}
No — one $\mathbf{W}^{(k)}$ per layer, shared by all nodes, like one CNN filter shared by
all pixels. That is *why* a GCN trained on some nodes generalizes to others and (with
care, Week 7) to new graphs. If nodes had private weights you would be back to Week 3's
shallow embeddings and their transductivity trap.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · “Deeper must be better”" icon="false"}
On Cora, a 2-layer GCN beats a 4-layer one. Each layer applies the low-pass operator once
more; @prp-lowpass says the signal converges to degree-scaled constants at rate
$|\mu_2|^k$. Depth in a GCN buys receptive field, not capacity — until Week 7's skip
connections change the arithmetic, graph depth ≠ CNN depth.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · A vs Ã in your code" icon="false"}
Forgetting self-loops ($\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$) silently discards
every node's own features at each layer *and* re-admits the $-1$ end of the spectrum
(part 3 of @prp-spectra fails without self-loops on bipartite structures — oscillation
instead of smoothing). Forgetting the $-1/2$ powers, or applying $\mathbf{D}^{-1}$ on one side only,
silently changes the operator's spectrum and its fixed point. Lab 6's assertions check
your $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ against a hand-computed case *before* you train — adopt that habit.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · “The spectral derivation is how GCNs work”" icon="false"}
The spectral story is a *derivation path* and an analysis lens, not the runtime: no
eigendecomposition happens in a GCN (that is @prp-poly's whole point). Conversely, don't
discard it — "GCN = low-pass filter" is the sharpest one-line summary of the model's
bias, and it predicts exactly when the GCN fails (heterophily, long-range dependencies).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Reporting a GNN win without the MLP baseline" icon="false"}
The 82% means nothing without the 60%. Every graph-ML claim you ever make should carry a
structure-blind baseline; on some datasets (and some industry tables) the MLP wins, and
finding that out *after* deployment is embarrassing. Lab 6 makes you produce both
numbers — and the SGC ablation, which tells you how much of the win was the *filter*
rather than the *network*.
:::

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Conceptual — The message-passing definition requires AGGREGATE to be permutation invariant. What concretely breaks if it is not? Give a function that violates it.</summary>
If AGGREGATE depends on neighbor order (e.g. an LSTM over the neighbor list, or "take the
first neighbor's vector"), the same graph stored with a different node ordering produces
different embeddings — the model's predictions become a function of storage layout, and
the equivariance proof of @thm-equiv fails at the step where the multiset is assumed orderless.
(GraphSAGE's LSTM aggregator really has this flaw; its authors shuffle neighbors to make
the model *learn* approximate invariance — Week 7.)
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand-simulation — In the hand-simulation example's graph, run a second layer with the same rule and weights, starting from h⁽¹⁾ = (3, 1, 3.5, 0). What is h_D⁽²⁾, and what happened to it?</summary>
$h_D^{(2)} = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathrm{mean}(h_B^{(1)}) + h_D^{(1)}) = \mathrm{ReLU}(1 + 0) = 1$.
$D$'s value was erased by the first layer's ReLU, and in the second layer it is entirely
reconstructed from its neighbor: after two rounds $D$'s representation carries no trace of
$x_D$ — a tiny preview of how information about the self can wash out.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Derivation — Prove part 2 of the spectra proposition yourself: every eigenvalue of a row-stochastic matrix lies in [−1, 1]. Where did you use nonnegativity?</summary>
For any eigenpair $(\lambda, \mathbf{v})$, pick the index $u$ with the largest $|v_u|$;
then $|\lambda||v_u| = |\sum_v P_{uv} v_v| \le \sum_v P_{uv} |v_v| \le |v_u| \sum_v P_{uv} = |v_u|$,
so $|\lambda| \le 1$. Nonnegativity is used in the first inequality (triangle inequality
with nonnegative weights); row sums equal to one in the last step. This is the same
argument that made PageRank's power iteration converge in Week 2.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Conceptual — Your friend says: "GCN needs the Laplacian eigendecomposition, so it can't scale." What exactly is wrong?</summary>
The eigendecomposition appears only in the *derivation* (@thm-gcn); the runtime layer is
$\sigma(\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W})$ with sparse $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ — cost
$O(m d' + n d d')$ per layer by the §2 accounting, no spectra computed ever. The valid
scaling concern is different: full-batch propagation touches the whole graph each step
(Week 11).
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Derivation — Where exactly does the equivariance theorem's proof use that σ is applied elementwise? Exhibit a σ for which equivariance fails.</summary>
The step $\sigma(\mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{M}) = \mathbf{P}_\pi \sigma(\mathbf{M})$: an
elementwise function commutes with any rearrangement of entries. A counterexample must
address positions: e.g. $\sigma(\mathbf{M}) = \mathbf{M}$ with row 1 zeroed ("mute the
first-stored node"). Which node is muted then depends on storage order, breaking
equivariance. The lesson: any operation that singles out node *indices* (not node
*values*) is illegal — the same rule the note after @thm-equiv states.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · Spectra — Compute the frequency response of the two-layer (linear) GCN, i.e. of Â², in terms of the eigenvalues μᵢ. Which components survive two layers best, and at what rate does a component with μ = 0.9 vs μ = 0.3 decay after k layers?</summary>
$\hat{\mathbf{A}}^2 = \sum_i \mu_i^2 \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top$ — response
$\mu_i^2$. Components near $\mu = 1$ (smooth, low-frequency) survive; after $k$ layers a
component decays as $\mu^k$: $0.9^k$ halves roughly every 6–7 layers, $0.3^k$ is at 1%
of its energy by $k = 4$. This is @prp-lowpass in numbers: mid- and high-frequency
structure is effectively deleted within a few layers.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Complexity — For ogbn-products (n ≈ 2.4M, m ≈ 62M, d = 100, hidden 128): how many multiply–adds does one GCN layer cost with sparse Â, and how much memory would a dense Â need?</summary>
Sparse: propagation $O(m d') \approx 62\text{M} \times 128 \approx 7.9$G multiply–adds,
mixing $O(n d d') \approx 2.4\text{M} \times 100 \times 128 \approx 30.7$G — about 39G
total, GPU-feasible. Dense $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$: $n^2 = 5.8 \times 10^{12}$ float32 entries
≈ 23 TB — not storable. Sparsity is the difference between "a big matmul" and
"impossible", which is why Week 11 exists (even the sparse full-batch pass runs out of
*activation* memory first).
</details>

<details><summary>Q8 · Transfer — Cora's citation graph is homophilous. Describe a node-classification graph where GCN's low-pass bias actively hurts, and name one repair from later weeks.</summary>
Any heterophilous graph — e.g. a dating network with gender labels, protein interaction
roles, or fraudster–victim transaction graphs: connected nodes tend to have *different*
labels, so averaging neighbors destroys the signal — in spectral terms, the label signal
lives at high frequencies, exactly where @prp-lowpass says the GCN attenuates. Repairs
previewed later: separate self/neighbor weights (GraphSAGE, Week 7), attention that can
down-weight neighbors (GAT, Week 7), or filters that pass high frequencies (the
$w_1 > 0$ region in Figure 4's filter mode — spectral methods, Week 13).
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **Neural message passing** (@def-mp, @eq-w06-mp) — message → aggregate → update over a neighborhood multiset.
- **Computation tree** (@def-w06-comp-tree) — the $k$-hop neighborhood unrolled.
- **Receptive field** (@def-w06-receptive) — the input nodes that can influence an output.
- **Basic GNN layer** (@def-basic) — separate self/neighbor weights; spectrum explodes unnormalized (@prp-spectra).
- **Normalization** (@eq-w06-mean, @eq-w06-sym) — mean vs symmetric degree-discounting.
- **GCN layer** (@def-gcn, @eq-w06-gcn) — symmetric normalization plus self-loops, one learned matrix per layer (@alg-w06-gcn-forward).
- **Graph Fourier transform** (@def-gft) — signals in the Laplacian's eigenbasis (@prp-freq, @eq-w06-tv).
- **Spectral / polynomial filter** (@eq-w06-filter, @prp-poly) — rescale frequency components; polynomial ⇒ local and cheap.
- **Renormalization trick** (@thm-gcn) — self-loops *before* normalizing; spectrum $(-1, 1]$ instead of $[0, 2]$.
- **Low-pass filtering / oversmoothing** (@eq-w06-response, @prp-lowpass) — the GCN's bias, collapsing at rate $|\mu_2|^k$; SGC (@alg-w06-sgc) deletes the network.
- **Permutation invariance / equivariance** (@def-perm, @thm-equiv) — storage order is not information.
:::
